cards.title: 3.1.1 Crops
body: Describe the major morphological differences between monocots and dicots.
Flowering plants (Angiosperms) are divided into two groups, namely monocots and dicots.
Monocot seeds have one “seed leaf” termed a cotyledon.
Classify the collection into dicots and monocots.

cards.title: 3.1.2 Photosynthesis
body: During photosynthesis, light energy from the sun is transformed into chemical energy that can be stored and transported in plants.
All green plants will grow only in the presence of light as light is required for photosynthesis.
During photosynthesis, the light energy is converted into chemical energy, which results in carbohydrates.
Chlorophyll absorbs the violet-blue and red part of the light spectrum.

cards.title: 3.1.3 The Soil–Water-Atmosphere-Plant Relationship
body: More than 80 percent of the essential plant nutrients are derived from soil.
Macronutrients or major nutrients: These nutrients are used by plants in relatively large quantities.
Macronutrients include nine elements: oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur.
Out of the major nutrients, namely nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are known as primary nutrients and the remaining as secondary nutrients.

cards.title: 3.1.4 The Functions of Macronutrients
body: N deficiency causes reduced growth and pale yellowish green leaves.
The older leaves turn yellowish first since the N is readily moved from the old leaves to the new growth.
Too much N can cause as much harm as too little.
An excess of N usually occurs when concentrated chemical forms of nitrogen fertilizers are used.

cards.title: 3.1.5 Soil Factors
body: The moisture lost through transpiration is made up only by absorbing water from the soil.
The important functions of water in the plant systems are to give turgidity and keep them erect; it regulates the temperature in the plant system; it acts as a solvent and nutrient carrier.
Indirectly, the water present in the soil helps the plant in many ways.

Soil air or oxygen is useful in increasing the nutrientavailability of the soil by breaking down the insoluble minerals into soluble salts; decomposing plant and animal remains and bringing about nitrifying and nitrogen-fixing processes by bacteria.

cards.title: 3.1.6 Water
body: Explain the effect of different climatic types on crop production and the measures to be taken.

cards.title: 3.1.7 Climatic Factors
body: More specifically climate is the general state of the atmosphere over a long period.
Climates result from energy and mass exchange within the atmosphere and between the atmosphere and the Earth’s surface.
Climate affects the pattern of vegetation, soils and water resources.
The major elements of climate that affect plant growth are rainfall, temperature, light, wind and humidity.

cards.title: 3.1.8 Seed
body: In some species the seeds have an endosperm, which is a storage tissue.
In others the cotyledons are the storage tissues.
Seed types in which the cotyledon is the storage tissue are called dicotyledons (dicots).
Seed types that have a welldeveloped endosperm and used as storage tissue are known as monocotyledons (monocots).

cards.title: Study steps
body: 1. Read the key definition cards once without notes.
2. Cover the examples and say the rule in your own words.
3. Do the unit exercise; check each why-step before the next question.
4. Replay the match game until you can finish it without peeking.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: What is the primary function of the xylem vascular tissue in plants?

steps.text: **Reasoning**
Xylem is a specialized vascular tissue in plants responsible for transporting water and dissolved inorganic nutrients absorbed by roots upward to the leaves.
Phloem transports organic sugars downward.
**Conclusion**
Therefore, the correct answer is **To transport water and dissolved minerals from roots to leaves.**

cards.answer: To transport water and dissolved minerals from roots to leaves.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which plant macronutrient is highly vital for seed germination, root development, and flower production, often causing purplish leaf margins when deficient?

steps.text: **Reasoning**
Phosphorus (P) is a primary macronutrient critical for energy storage, root development, and flower/seed production.
Its deficiency is characterized by stunted growth and a distinct dull bluish-green leaf color turning purplish.
**Conclusion**
Thus, the nutrient is **Phosphorus (P)**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What type of germination occurs when the cotyledons are carried above the soil surface due to hypocotyl elongation?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
In epigeal germination, the hypocotyl elongates and bends, pulling the cotyledons above the soil surface into the light. In hypogeal germination, the cotyledons remain below ground.

**Conclusion**
Therefore, the correct germination type is **Epigeal**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following field crops is a native pulse (legume) domesticated in the Abyssinian center of diversity?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
According to N.I. Vavilov's classification, the Abyssinian center is the center of origin for pulses like chickpea, field pea, and lentil. Teff is a cereal, sesame is an oil crop, and maize originated in Central America.

**Conclusion**
The native pulse is the **Chickpea**.

cards.title: 3.2.1 Introduction
body: Originally, the growth of plants was limited to certain geographic areas of the globe.
Later, plants started to disperse to other regions.
The Russian scientist, NI Vavilov divided the world into six to nine centres of origin.
Taff and Niger seed are also domesticated in this centre.

cards.title: 3.2.2 The Classification of Field Crops
body: Field crops are classified based on agronomic, or special purpose or and growth habits.
Cereals: These are crops grown for their edible seeds.
Pulses: These are leguminous plants that produce edible seeds such as beans, peas, lentils, etc.
Pulses are rich in protein, have the ability to fix nitrogen from the air and are important sources of income.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: One of the following fertilizers has the **highest** phosphate content.
cards.why: Di-ammonium phosphate (DAP) is a concentrated phosphate fertilizer. It typically contains about 46% phosphorus ($$P_2O_5$$) and 18% nitrogen. Urea is a nitrogen fertilizer, while the others are organic sources with much lower nutrient concentrations.

cards.title: The season in order — never skip a step on the paper
body: Site → land prep → fertiliser → sowing → weed/pest/disease → harvest → thresh & store.

cards.title: The season in order — never skip a step on the paper
body:
- **Site:** depth, slope, previous crop, water, access.
- **Land prep:** plough/hoe to a fine enough tilth, on contour if sloped, bury residues or compost.
- **Fertiliser:** organic (manure, compost) feeds soil life; mineral NPK corrects a measured shortage. Split nitrogen so rain does not wash it all at once.
- **Sowing:** right date (rain), depth, rate, method — broadcasting, drilling/rows, transplanting for some horticulture.
- **Protection:** weeds steal light and water; insects and diseases need scouting + resistant varieties + sanitation + only then chemicals if available and safe.
- **Harvest / store:** dry enough grain, clean store, no holes for weevils. Wet grain in a bag is how a good season becomes a loss.

cards.title: 3.3.1 Site Selection
body: Site selection is an important step in the identification of suitable lands for different types of crop.
Crops are grown best in areas of their adaptation.
Most crop species can be successfully produced in soil types that are well drained and productive.
Favourable climate and adequate water supply are required for optimal production.

cards.title: 3.3.2 Land Preparation
body: Land preparation is a requirement for crop production.
The timing and the quality of land preparation influence the growth of crops.
Poor and untimely land preparation may cause serious weed problems and may lead to soil erosion.
Physical loosening of the soil can be carried out in a range of cultivation operations by hand, animaldrawn ploughs or machines.

cards.title: 3.3.3 Fertilizer
body: Plants cannot live without the 16 essential elements.
Plants obtain these nutritional elements from the soil.
If the soil is deficient in any of these elements due to natural conditions, leaching or intensive crop cultivation, they must be replaced in with fertilizer.
Examples of inorganic fertilizers are: urea and di-ammonium phosphate (DAP).

cards.title: 3.3.4 Sowing
body: Sowing of crops is influenced by the nature of the precipitation, temperature, occurrence of diseases and pests as well as marketing.
On a seasonal basis the crop should be planted at a time when there is enough subsequent rainfall.
Planting in moist soil allows rapid seed germination or sprouting.
Under semi-arid conditions, early sowing contributes to efficient water use.

cards.title: 3.3.5 Methods of Sowing
body: Seed is sown into the soil using different mechanical planters or by hand.
Generally, three sowing methods are used: broadcasting, row planting and sowing in drills.

Row planting has an advantage because the amount of seed required is less; it is also possible carry out inter-row cultivation and spraying chemicals without damaging the plant and the yield is also better.
Under dry land conditions, farmers traditionally use high seed rates for certain crops.

cards.title: 3.3.6 Weeds, Insects and Diseases
body: As long as a plant is growing at a place and time without interfering with man’s activities, all unwanted plants may not be weeds for example Cynodon dactylon may be one of the worst grass weeds but it is grown for use as a valuable hay or fodder.

Several disadvantages result from the effect of weeds: yield losses, insect and disease incidence, poor quality of produce, human and animal health problems, water contamination and reduction in land value.
Unit Three Crop Production a source of animal feed, manure or compost and have medicinal values.
Additional benefits are that some weed plants used for oil extraction, construction (huts), soil and water conservation, etc.

cards.title: 3.3.7 Cultivation
body: List them and give the reasons why this is done.
Cultivation is an inter-tillage operation performed when the crop reaches certain growth stages, particularly knee height.
During cultivation the upper surface only of the soil is loosened.
Cultivation promotes nitrification in the soil, controls weeds; conserves soil moisture by preventing runoff and providing sufficient aeration.

cards.title: 3.3.8 Harvesting
body: Harvesting is the deliberate detachment of the edible or usable part of the crop for use as an agricultural product.
In modern agriculture, harvesting may include cutting, threshing of crops, separating crop from the debris, or cleaning using combined harvesters.
Premature and over-matured crops result in loss of yield quality, quantity or both.
The most common indicators for harvesting are when the crop changes its colour to brown or a yellowish colour.

cards.title: 3.3.9 Threshing and Storage of Field Crops
body: Seed-ageing or deterioration and loss of germination potential can be reduced by under proper storage conditions.
The factors affecting storage include: initial seed quality, moisture content, relative humidity, temperature and oxygen.
The rate of seed deterioration increases as the seed moisture content increases.
For example the optimum moisture level for soybeans is 7 per cent, for pulses approximately 10 per cent and for cereals it should not exceed 12.5 per cent.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which specialized branch of horticulture deals specifically with the study, production, and management of fruit crops?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Pomology is the branch of horticulture that focuses on the cultivation, physiology, and marketing of fruit crops (such as bananas, mangoes, and citrus). Olericulture deals with vegetables.

**Conclusion**
Therefore, the correct branch is **Pomology**.

As described, sunken beds (sunk $$10\text{ to }15\text{ cm}$$ below ground) are designed to capture and conserve soil moisture in arid and dry regions with limited rainfall. Raised beds are used for drainage.

cards.q: During seed bed preparation, the use of raised seed beds is important to
cards.why: Raised seed beds are elevated above the ground level. Their primary purpose is to improve soil drainage and aeration, preventing waterlogging which can rot sensitive seeds and young seedlings.

cards.title: Cropping systems · Mono-cropping
body: Same crop again and again. Simple, but pests and nutrient gaps build.

cards.title: Mixed / intercrop
body: Two species together. Insurance if one fails; pulses can feed cereals.

cards.title: Alley cropping
body: Crops between rows of trees/shrubs. Trees give mulch, fodder, some wood.

cards.title: Fallow
body: Rest the land so fertility and structure recover — only works if there is enough land.

cards.title: Rotation
body: Cereal → pulse → maybe a root or oil crop. Breaks pest cycles; pulses leave N.

cards.title: Rotation trick
body: Never “sorghum–sorghum–sorghum” as your ideal answer. Say *cereal then a legume* and name why (N + different pests).

cards.title: 3.4.1 Mono-cropping
body: The repetitive growing of the same crop grown alone in pure stand in the same piece of land is called mono-cropping.

cards.title: 3.4.2 Mixed Cropping
body: Growing two or more crops in the same land and in the same year without any particular raw arrangement is called mixed cropping.
Inter-cropping is one form of mixed cropping where two or more crops are grown on the same land and year in a particular arrangement.
Examples of the mixed cropping or inter-cropping system in Eritrea are sorghum and beans/cow pea; maize and potato, etc.
In mixed cropping or inter-cropping two products are obtained from the same piece of land.

cards.title: 3.4.3 Alley Cropping
body: The hedges are pruned prior to and periodically during cropping cycles to prevent shading of the companion crop.
The resultant prunings are then applied to the soil as green manure and/or mulch.
Hedgerows are allowed to grow freely to cover the land between cropping cycles.
Litter falling on the ground and prunings will provide mulch and nutrients will be retained in the soil when the mulch decomposes.

cards.title: 3.4.4 Fallowing
body: Fallowing is a type of crop rotation in which land is not farmed for more than one year.
The objective of this practice is to allow the soil time to restore its fertility.

cards.title: 3.4.5 Crop Rotation
body: When crop rotation involves the rotation of annual crops and perennial crops such as fruit trees, the cycle may take several years to complete.
In some cases it may take the form of shifting cultivation, and managed-tree fallow, including relay inter-cropping.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the standard recommended volumetric soil mix ratio for containerized nursery seedlings?

options.A: 1 part soil : 1 part compost : 1 part sand
options.B: 3 parts soil : 1 part compost : 1 part sand
options.C: 2 parts soil : 2 parts compost : 1 part sand
options.D: 5 parts soil : 1 part compost : 1 part sand
options.E: No mix, pure straight soil is best

cards.why:
**Reasoning**
According to the standard potting soil preparation, a high-quality mix consists of 3 parts garden soil (for structure), 1 part compost (for nutrients), and 1 part sand (for drainage).

**Conclusion**
Therefore, the correct ratio is **3 parts soil : 1 part compost : 1 part sand**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In vegetative propagation, what is the name of the upper section of a grafted plant that forms the new shoot system and holds the desired fruit traits?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
In a grafted plant, the scion is the upper stem portion containing buds that is inserted onto the rootstock. The scion develops into the shoot system and determines the fruit characteristics.

**Conclusion**
This upper section is the **Scion**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A major cropping system which growing of perennial trees with annual crops at the same time and place is known as _______________.
cards.why: **Alley cropping** is an agroforestry practice where perennial trees or shrubs are grown in rows, and annual agricultural crops are grown in the 'alleys' between those rows. This system helps in soil conservation and provides multiple sources of income.

cards.title: 3.5 Horticulture
body: Horticulture = fruits, vegetables, flowers, spices — usually more intensive, higher value, more water and labour per hectare, often started in a **nursery**.

cards.title: Nursery idea
body: Raise seedlings where you can water, shade and protect them, then transplant to the field. Site: near water, not waterlogged, fenced from goats, partial shade for delicate species.

cards.title: Vegetative propagation — keep the parent’s traits
head: Method
Memory hook
rows: A stick that grows roots (rose, some trees)
Bend a living stem into soil until it roots, then cut free
Join a good scion onto a tough rootstock (fruit trees)

cards.title: Mnemonic — C.L.D.G.
body: *Cut, Layer, Divide, Graft.* Seed = sexual (variation). These four = asexual (clone the mother).

body: After harvest, horticultural produce is alive and watery — shade, don’t bruise, move fast, some crops need curing. That is post-harvest handling; a beautiful tomato on the plant is worthless if it rots on the road.

cards.title: Quiz 3 — crops & horticulture
body: Based on Agricultural Science Technology for Grade 11, Ministry of Education, Eritrea (2011).

cards.title: 3.5.1 Introduction
body: Horticulture is a branch of agriculture, which involves the production and handling of horticultural crops and deals with activities related to protection and maintenance of the environment.
Others are used in traditional medicine to heal various diseases.
Commercial value: Horticultural plants form part of the trade between countries and are therefore earners of foreign exchange.
Vast quantities of plants are exported worldwide.

cards.title: 3.5.2 Production System in Horticulture
body: Depending on the production environment, horticulture production systems can be open fields, protected areas and hydroponics.
Based on the scale of production, horticultural production varies from few square metres in home gardens to thousands of hectares on large farms.

cards.title: 3.5.4 Site Selection
body: Describe the routine nursery management practices.
Seedbeds are used for sowing seeds or placing poly-tubes.
Raised seedbeds are used in areas where drainage is needed.
Sunken seedbeds are used when it is necessary to conserve moisture in places with low rainfall.

cards.title: 3.5.5 Nursery Practices
body: Vegetables and other annual crops are sown in seedbeds or seed boxes or in special containers known as plug trays.
Trees and shrubs are sown either directly in containers or first sown at high density in seedbeds or seed trays and later transplanted into containers.
After sowing, the seedbed or container is covered with mulch of grass or similar materials.
The mulch is removed soon after germination.

cards.title: 3.5.6 Vegetative Propagation
body: Vegetative propagation is the use of vegetative parts such as the stem, leaf and root to reproduce plants.
The lower section of the tree is known as rootstock.
The scion, which is the upper section of the tree forms the shoot system and is responsible for holding the desired plant characteristics.
The scion is the part of the new combination, which is inserted into another plant to produce branches, leaves and fruit of the desired plant.

cards.title: 3.5.7 Propagation by Cutting
body: Plants that are easily propagated by cutting include lantana, grape and coleus.
Stem cuttings are commonly used although roots have also been found to work well with some plants.
Rooting hormones speed up rooting and the cuttings can be inserted into a medium containing a suitable soil mix.
The medium should be well-drained and sterile.

cards.title: 3.5.8 Propagation by Layering
body: Branches of 1–2 cm in diameter are preferred.
The selected branch is girdled by removing a ring of bark 1–3 cm in width and about 15–30 cm from the terminal end of the branch.
The area, which is girdled is then covered with a ball of moist compost and rapped with a polyethylene sheeting or aluminium foil.
Mangos, rubber plants, crotons and camellias are examples of plants that can be propagated using this method.

cards.title: 3.5.9 Propagation by Division
body: Plants with multi-stem or clumping growth habit, offshoots, or with underground storage structures such as bulbs, corms, rhizomes and tubers are propagated by division.
Division involves cutting large clumps into smaller sections, making sure that each smaller clump has adequate amount of stems, leaves, roots and buds to survive transplanting.
Plants commonly propagated by division are banana, date palm, potato, garlic, ferns, orchids, daylilies, flowering bulbous plants, etc.
In propagation by division the new small corms are separated and used for producing new plants.

cards.title: 3.5.10 Cultural Field Practices for Horticultural Crops
body: Fruit trees are perennial crops, hence, once an orchard is established it is not easy to change it.
Vegetables also have a combination of economical and environmental requirements that ensure sustainable yield, easier management and profitability.
Any failure in satisfying such requirements may result in serious problems.
Terrain: Identify a suitable elevation and slope based on the requirement of the crop.

cards.title: 3.5.11 Land Preparation
body: Based on the plan, the seedbeds should be laid out and marked.
Proper spacing of the seedbeds is important to ease cultivation operations from the path (e.g. weeding).
Seedbeds are normally 1.0–1.2 m wide to facilitate routine operations.
Fences or hedges should be constructed around the garden to prevent destruction of the crops by animals.

cards.title: 3.5.12 Sowing and Transplanting
body: Varieties vary in the time take to maturity, resistance to disease, tolerance of heat, etc.
Unknown seeds should not be used for commercial purposes, even if they are provided free.
Germination test: Run germination test to find out if the seeds are viable.
Under hot and humid conditions, seeds deteriorate rapidly even if they are taken from a freshly opened, sealed can.

cards.title: 3.5.13 Post-harvest Handling
body: Good post-harvest handling will guarantee the products reach the consumer in good condition.
Consequently, farmers and all others involved in marketing of horticultural crops are advised to follow improved post-harvest handling practices to maintain higher incomes.
Inter-cropping, rotation, mulching, cutting and soft-woodcutting.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which vegetative propagation method is used for plants with hard woody stems, where a branch is girdled and wrapped in moist compost/moss while still attached to the mother plant?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Air layering is practiced on woody branches. It involves removing a ring of bark (girdling), wrapping the wound in moist compost/moss, wrapping it in plastic foil to trap moisture, and encouraging root formation while attached to the parent.

**Conclusion**
Therefore, the correct method is **Air layering**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following field crops is classified as an annual crop, completing its entire life cycle within one single cropping season?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Wheat is an annual crop because it completes its life cycle from seed to seed in a single cropping season. Sugar beet is biennial, and sugarcane, coffee, and alfalfa are perennials.

**Conclusion**
Thus, the annual crop is **Wheat**.

cards.q: The method of propagation by which new plants are formed while attached to mother plant is known as;
cards.why: Layering is a vegetative propagation method where a stem is encouraged to develop roots while still attached to the parent (mother) plant. Once roots are established, the new plant is detached to grow independently.

glossary.meaning: Cereals are the main sources of carbohydrates for humans.
Eritrea is a centre of diversity for a number of crop species.
Site selection is an important step in the identification of suitable lands for different types of crop.
Land preparation is a requirement for crop production.
Cultivation is an inter-tillage operation performed when the crop reaches certain growth stages, particularly knee height.
Harvesting is the deliberate detachment of the edible or usable part of the crop for use as an agricultural product.
Crop rotation is a system of land-use practice in which crops are grown in sequence on the same piece of land.
Mixed cropping or inter-cropping is a system of growing two or more crops on the same land.
Horticulture is a branch of agriculture, which involves the production and handling of horticultural crops and deals with activities related to protection and maintenance of the environment.
Vegetative propagation is the use of vegetative parts such as the stem, leaf and root to reproduce plants.
Budding is the most commonly used technique for propagating new plants, but it is sometimes used to top-work existing trees to a new variety.
Layering is a method of propagation by which new plants are formed while attached to mother plant.

tips.text: Cultivated plants are divided into field and horticultural crops.
Flowering plants are divided into monocots and dicots.
Plants can be divided into sexual, reproductive and vegetative parts.
Soil sustains plant life by providing nutrients, water, air and support.
Sixteen elements are essential for healthy growth and development of plants.
The elements are classified into macronutrients or major nutrients and micronutrients or minor plant nutrients.
Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are primary nutrients among the macronutrients or major nutrients.
What do you understand by the term “field crops”? 2.
How can you justify that Eritrea is a centre of origin or diversity of many crops?
Originally, the growth of plants was limited to certain geographic areas of the globe.
Cropping systems · Mono-cropping: Same crop again and again. Simple, but pests and nutrient gaps build.
Mixed / intercrop: Two species together. Insurance if one fails; pulses can feed cereals.
Alley cropping: Crops between rows of trees/shrubs. Trees give mulch, fodder, some wood.
Fallow: Rest the land so fertility and structure recover — only works if there is enough land.
Rotation: Cereal → pulse → maybe a root or oil crop. Breaks pest cycles; pulses leave N.

questions.q: Complete the photosynthesis equation that your unit uses to explain how a cereal crop such as sorghum builds its food: $$\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{______} \xrightarrow{\text{______}} \text{Sugar} + \text{______}$$ Fill in the three blanks in order, and name the pigment written above the arrow.
questions.answer: Blank 1 = Light Energy; Blank 2 = Chlorophyll; Blank 3 = O2, i.e. $$\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Light Energy} \xrightarrow{\text{Chlorophyll}} \text{Sugar} + \text{O}_2$$. The pigment above the arrow is chlorophyll.
why: **Recall the unit equation.** The unit defines photosynthesis as the biological process in which light energy is transformed into chemical energy, and writes it as $$\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Light Energy} \xrightarrow{\text{Chlorophyll}} \text{Sugar} + \text{O}_2$$.
**Fill the first blank (energy input).** The only input still missing from the left-hand side is the energy source, so the first blank is Light Energy (sunlight).

**Fill the second blank (the substance above the arrow).** The unit places Chlorophyll above the reaction arrow. Chlorophyll is the green pigment of the leaf (the leaf is the site of photosynthesis) that captures the light energy needed to drive the reaction.
**Fill the third blank (by-product).** The right-hand side already shows Sugar; the second product released by the plant is oxygen gas, so the third blank is O2.

**Conclude.** Blank 1 = Light Energy, Blank 2 = Chlorophyll, Blank 3 = O2, giving the complete equation $$\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Light Energy} \xrightarrow{\text{Chlorophyll}} \text{Sugar} + \text{O}_2$$.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A farmer in Akordat wants to explain to a neighbour why a maize field must be exposed to sunlight. Complete the statement using the unit equation: in photosynthesis, $$\text{CO}_2$$ and $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ are joined using ______ energy in the presence of the pigment ______ to produce ______ and oxygen.
questions.answer: Light (solar) energy; chlorophyll; sugar. Full statement: $$\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Light Energy} \xrightarrow{\text{Chlorophyll}} \text{Sugar} + \text{O}_2$$.
why: **Write the unit equation.** $$\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Light Energy} \xrightarrow{\text{Chlorophyll}} \text{Sugar} + \text{O}_2$$.

**Match each blank to a term in the equation.** The energy term on the left is Light Energy; the term written above the arrow is Chlorophyll; the carbon-containing product on the right (besides O2) is Sugar.

**State the completed statement.** Carbon dioxide and water are joined using light energy in the presence of chlorophyll to produce sugar and oxygen, so shaded maize cannot carry out this process normally.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: Identify the three raw materials/inputs of photosynthesis listed in the unit equation and name the two products formed. Then state in one sentence why the unit calls photosynthesis the process that 'transforms light energy into chemical energy'.
questions.answer: Inputs: carbon dioxide ($$\text{CO}_2$$), water ($$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$) and light energy. Products: sugar and oxygen ($$\text{O}_2$$). It is called a transformation of energy because light energy is captured by chlorophyll and stored in the chemical bonds of the sugar produced.
why: **List the inputs.** Left of the arrow the unit gives three inputs: carbon dioxide, water and light energy.
**List the products.** Right of the arrow the products are sugar and oxygen gas.

**Explain the energy wording.** The unit states that light energy is transformed into chemical energy; chlorophyll traps the light and the energy ends up stored in the sugar, which is why the sugar is the plant's food.

questions.q: A farmer in the Eritrean highlands sows two plots on the same day: Plot A with field peas and Plot B with common beans. Several days later the farmer notices that in Plot B the cotyledons have been pushed above the soil surface, while in Plot A the cotyledons are still below the soil. (a) Name the type of germination shown in Plot A and in Plot B. (b) Explain which elongating structure is responsible in each case. (c) In which plot, if any, do the cotyledons act as the first photosynthetic leaves?
questions.answer: (a) Plot A (peas) = hypogeal germination; Plot B (common beans) = epigeal germination. (b) Hypogeal: the epicotyl elongates while the cotyledons stay below the soil. Epigeal: the hypocotyl elongates and pulls the cotyledons above the soil. (c) Only in Plot B (epigeal), where the cotyledons act as the first photosynthetic leaves.
why: **Recall the two germination types.** The unit defines two types based on cotyledon movement: hypogeal germination, in which the cotyledons remain below the soil surface while the epicotyl elongates (peas, broad beans), and epigeal germination, in which the hypocotyl elongates and pulls the cotyledons above the soil surface (common beans, castor oil).
**Classify Plot A (field peas).** In Plot A the cotyledons stay below the soil; peas are named in the unit as an example of hypogeal germination.
**Classify Plot B (common beans).** In Plot B the cotyledons are carried above the surface; common beans are the unit's example of epigeal germination.
**Name the elongating structures.** Plot A (hypogeal): the epicotyl elongates and the cotyledons remain underground. Plot B (epigeal): the hypocotyl elongates, lifting the cotyledons out of the soil.

**Decide where cotyledons photosynthesise.** Only in Plot B, because the unit states that in epigeal germination the cotyledons are pulled above the soil surface where they act as the first photosynthetic leaves.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A school garden in Asmara plants broad beans in one bed and castor oil in another. For each crop, state the type of germination, say whether the cotyledons finish above or below the soil surface, and name the structure whose elongation decides the position of the cotyledons.
questions.answer: Broad beans: hypogeal germination, cotyledons remain below the soil, epicotyl elongates. Castor oil: epigeal germination, cotyledons are pulled above the soil, hypocotyl elongates.
why: **Apply the unit definitions.** Hypogeal = cotyledons remain below the surface while the epicotyl elongates; epigeal = the hypocotyl elongates and pulls the cotyledons above the surface.
**Match broad beans.** The unit lists broad beans under hypogeal germination, so their cotyledons stay below the soil and the epicotyl is the elongating structure.
**Match castor oil.** The unit lists castor oil under epigeal germination, so the hypocotyl elongates and the cotyledons are carried above the soil.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: Explain why the seed of a crop such as maize can germinate to a strong seedling only when three environmental conditions are present. Name the three conditions given in the unit and state the specific role of each one.
questions.answer: The three conditions are adequate water (softens the seed coat and activates the enzymes), oxygen (needed for aerobic respiration) and optimum temperature (generally $$10^\circ\text{C}$$ to $$35^\circ\text{C}$$, with about $$20^\circ\text{C}$$ optimum for most crops). Without all three, the embryo cannot resume growth and germination fails or is weak.
why: **State what germination is.** The unit defines germination as the process by which a seed embryo wakes from dormancy and begins to grow into a seedling.
**Name the three environmental conditions.** Successful germination requires adequate water, oxygen and an optimum temperature.

**Give the role of each condition.** Water softens the seed coat and activates enzymes; oxygen supports aerobic respiration; temperature must be in the range of about $$10^\circ\text{C}$$ to $$35^\circ\text{C}$$ with $$20^\circ\text{C}$$ being optimum for most crops.
**Conclude.** All three conditions must be met together, which is why waterlogged or very cold soil gives poor emergence even when good seed is sown.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A wheat crop near Keren shows a pale yellowish-green colour. An extension agent observes that the symptom is visible on the old, lower leaves while the young upper leaves are still green, and explains that this happens because nitrogen is highly mobile in the plant. According to the unit, why does a nitrogen shortage affect the old, lower leaves before the young leaves?

options.A: Because nitrogen is immobile in the plant, so it stays fixed inside the leaves that first received it
options.B: Because the plant moves nitrogen out of the old leaves to support new growth, and those old leaves are the first to run short
options.C: Because old leaves have the smallest leaf area, so they lose nutrients to the soil before the young leaves do
options.D: Because old leaves receive the least sunlight, so their chlorophyll breaks down before that of the upper leaves

why: **Recall the unit's Pro-Tip.** The unit's Pro-Tip states that nitrogen is highly mobile in plants and that when a deficiency occurs the plant moves nitrogen from old leaves to support new growth.

**Link mobility to the visible pattern.** Because nitrogen can be withdrawn from the old, lower leaves and redirected to the growing points, the older leaves are the first to fall short of nitrogen and therefore the first to show the pale yellowish-green deficiency colour.
**Check option A.** A contradicts the unit: nitrogen is described as highly mobile, not immobile, so A is false.

**Check option C.** Nutrient shortage is caused by internal redistribution to new growth, not by old leaves having a smaller area or by loss of nutrients to the soil; no such process is given in the unit, so C is false.
**Check option D.** The unit gives no role for sunlight differences among leaves in nitrogen deficiency; the symptom is explained by nutrient mobility, not by a light gradient, so D is false.
**Conclude.** Only option B states the unit's reason: nitrogen is moved out of the old leaves to support new growth, so the old leaves yellow first.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: A farmer in the Eritrean highlands tells an extension agent: 'My barley leaves are small and dull bluish-green with purplish tints, and the roots look weak.' Which nutrient deficiency in the unit table best explains this description?
why: **Read the described symptoms.** Small, dull bluish-green leaves with purplish tints plus poor root growth are the field signs reported.

**Match against the unit table.** The table gives phosphorus deficiency as 'small, dull bluish-green leaves with purplish tints', and phosphorus is described as aiding seed germination, root growth and flowering.

**Eliminate the other options.** Nitrogen gives pale yellowish-green older leaves; potassium gives scorched brown tips and margins; calcium gives poorly developed hooked leaf tips and weak root tips. None matches bluish-green purplish leaves.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: Which statement about the nutrient requirements of crop plants is correct according to the unit?
questions.answer: C. Plants require $$16$$ essential elements, and micronutrients such as Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, B, Mo and Cl are needed in tiny amounts although they are equally essential
why: **State the unit's total requirement.** The unit states that for healthy growth plants require $$16$$ essential elements, divided into macronutrients and micronutrients.
**Check option A.** A reverses the definition: micronutrients (trace elements) are required in tiny amounts, not in large quantities, so A is false.
**Check option B.** The unit states that carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are obtained from air and water, so they are not applied as fertilizer; B is false.
**Check option D.** The unit classifies nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium as primary nutrients and calcium, magnesium and sulphur as secondary nutrients, which is the reverse of D, so D is false.

**Confirm option C.** C correctly combines the figure of $$16$$ essential elements with the unit's list of micronutrients (Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, B, Mo, Cl) and their tiny but equally essential requirement, so C is the only correct statement.

questions.q: A sorghum field of $$1$$ hectare near Keren has a plant population of $$30{,}000$$ plants. On average, each plant carries $$3$$ heads (panicles), and each head contains $$168$$ grains. Calculate the total number of grains produced in the hectare and express your answer in scientific notation. Then state, in one sentence, what this figure represents for the farmer.
questions.answer: Total grains = $$30{,}000 \times 3 \times 168 = 15{,}120{,}000$$ grains per hectare = $$1.512 \times 10^{7}$$ grains. This is the hectare's total grain (potential seed) harvest from the sorghum crop.
why: **Name the quantities given.** Plant population = $$30{,}000$$ plants/ha; heads per plant = $$3$$; grains per head = $$168$$; area = $$1$$ ha. The unit classifies sorghum as a cereal grown for its edible starchy seeds, so the harvestable unit is the grain.

**Choose the working formula.** Total grains = plant population x heads per plant x grains per head, i.e. the seed output is built up from the number of seed-bearing plants and the seeds carried by each head.
**Calculate the grains per plant.** $$3 \times 168 = 504$$ grains per plant.
**Multiply by the plant population.** $$30{,}000 \times 504 = 15{,}120{,}000$$ grains per hectare.
**Convert to scientific notation.** Place one digit before the decimal point: $$15{,}120{,}000 = 1.512 \times 10^{7}$$ grains.

**Interpret the result.** The figure is the total number of grains (potential seeds) the hectare can yield; because it is a cereal, these grains are the starchy food harvest the farmer sells or stores, and the same figure is the largest possible number of seeds available for sowing the next season.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A sesame field of $$1$$ hectare in the lowlands of Eritrea carries $$40{,}000$$ plants. Each plant bears on average $$3$$ capsules, and each capsule contains $$50$$ seeds. Find the total number of seeds produced per hectare and write it in scientific notation.
why: **List the data.** Plants per hectare = $$40{,}000$$; capsules per plant = $$3$$; seeds per capsule = $$50$$. The unit lists sesame as an oil crop, so its harvested propagules are the seeds.
**State the formula.** Total seeds = plant population x capsules per plant x seeds per capsule.
**Substitute and multiply step by step.** $$3 \times 50 = 150$$ seeds per plant; $$40{,}000 \times 150 = 6{,}000{,}000$$ seeds per hectare.
**Convert to scientific notation.** $$6{,}000{,}000 = 6 \times 10^{6}$$ seeds per hectare.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A field pea plot of $$1$$ hectare on a farm near Mendefera has $$250{,}000$$ plants. Each plant forms $$4$$ pods, and each pod contains $$5$$ seeds. (a) Calculate the total number of seeds per hectare. (b) If the farmer must keep $$20\%$$ of these seeds for sowing next season, how many seeds are kept for sowing?
why: **List the data.** Plants per hectare = $$250{,}000$$; pods per plant = $$4$$; seeds per pod = $$5$$; sowing reserve = $$20\%$$. Field peas are listed in the unit as a pulse grown for protein-rich seeds.
**Formula for total seed number.** Total seeds = plant population x pods per plant x seeds per pod.
**Compute part (a).** $$4 \times 5 = 20$$ seeds per plant; $$250{,}000 \times 20 = 5{,}000{,}000$$ seeds per hectare.
**Compute part (b).** Sowing reserve = $$\frac{20}{100} \times 5{,}000{,}000 = 1{,}000{,}000$$ seeds, which can also be written $$1 \times 10^{6}$$ seeds.
**Interpret.** The farmer harvests 5 million seeds and must set aside 1 million of them as the seed stock for the next planting, leaving 4 million seeds as the food/grain share.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: An agricultural extension officer working with farmers in the Eritrean highlands and western lowlands is preparing a planting plan based on the agronomic classification of field crops given in the unit. The crops under consideration are: teff, niger seed (nihug), faba bean, cotton, sorghum, sesame and sugarcane. (a) Sort all seven crops into their correct agronomic groups (cereals, pulses, industrial crops, forage crops). (b) Name the sub-groups of the industrial crops into which niger seed, cotton and sugarcane fall. (c) The officer advises a farmer who grew sorghum this season to rotate it next season with faba bean rather than with another cereal. Using the unit's description of pulses, justify this advice with one biological reason. (d) Which of the seven crops is a native of the Abyssinian center of diversity, and what does teff's origin there tell us about the crop?
questions.answer: (a) Cereals: teff and sorghum. Pulses: faba bean. Industrial crops: niger seed (oil), sesame (oil), cotton (fiber) and sugarcane (sugar). Forage crops: none of the seven crops listed. (b) Niger seed and sesame = oil crops; cotton = fiber crop; sugarcane = sugar crop. (c) Pulses such as faba bean are leguminous plants able to fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil, so a faba bean crop restores the nitrogen that the sorghum cereal removed, improving soil fertility for the next crop. (d) Teff is native to the Abyssinian center of diversity (Eritrean Highlands); because its wild progenitor Eragrostis pilosa is native there, teff was domesticated locally thousands of years ago.
why: **Recall the four agronomic groups.** The unit classifies field crops as cereals (grown for edible starchy seeds, rich in carbohydrates), pulses (leguminous plants grown for protein-rich seeds and valued for fixing atmospheric nitrogen), industrial crops (raw materials for industries), and forage crops (grown as livestock feed, preserved as hay or silage or grazed).
**Assign the cereals.** Teff (Eragrostis tef) and sorghum are stated in the unit to be cereals because they are grown for their edible starchy seeds; the unit's cereal examples include both.
**Assign the pulse.** Faba bean (Vicia faba) is listed in the unit's crop table as a pulse (legume), so it forms the single pulse entry among the seven crops.

**Assign the industrial crops and their sub-groups.** Niger seed (nihug) and sesame are oil crops, cotton is a fiber crop and sugarcane is a sugar crop, so all four are industrial crops. The unit's sub-groups are oil crops (sesame, linseed), sugar crops (sugarcane, sugar beet) and fiber crops (cotton, sisal).

**Check for forage crops.** None of the seven crops is described in the unit as a forage crop: forage crops are grown specifically as livestock feed and conserved as hay or silage. The forage group therefore has no member in this list, which is an important negative finding for the officer's plan.

**Justify the rotation advice (part c).** The unit states that pulses are leguminous plants valued for their ability to fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil. Sorghum, as a cereal, takes nutrients out of the soil during the season, whereas a faba bean crop adds nitrogen to the soil. Rotating sorghum with faba bean therefore restores soil nitrogen and improves the fertility of the field for the following cereal crop.

**Identify the Abyssinian native and interpret it (part d).** The unit's table gives teff's native center of diversity as the Abyssinian Center (Eritrean Highlands); niger seed, barley, emmer wheat, linseed, safflower, chickpea, lentil and sesame are also named as crops domesticated there. The unit's Did You Know note adds that the wild progenitor of cultivated teff, Eragrostis pilosa, is native to this center, which confirms that teff was domesticated locally thousands of years ago.

**Conclude the classification.** Cereals: teff, sorghum. Pulse: faba bean. Industrial crops (oil): niger seed, sesame; (fiber): cotton; (sugar): sugarcane. Forage: none of the seven. Rotation with faba bean is justified because pulses fix atmospheric nitrogen, and teff belongs to the Abyssinian center of diversity, confirming local domestication.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A farmer in the Eritrean highlands plans a four-field rotation and can choose from barley, linseed, chickpea and sisal. (a) Classify each crop into its agronomic group and, for any industrial crop, name its sub-group. (b) Which two of these crops would you recommend the farmer grow in order to add nitrogen to the soil, and why? (c) State one reason from the unit why a crop such as sisal is described as a fiber crop rather than a cereal.
questions.answer: (a) Barley = cereal; linseed = industrial crop, oil crop; chickpea = pulse; sisal = industrial crop, fiber crop. (b) Chickpea would be recommended, because it is a leguminous pulse valued for fixing atmospheric nitrogen in the soil; linseed is an oil crop and does not add nitrogen. (c) Sisal is grown as a raw material for industry (its fiber), whereas cereals are grown for their edible starchy seeds, so the two crops belong to different agronomic groups.
why: **Recall the classification criteria.** Cereals are grown for edible starchy seeds rich in carbohydrates; pulses are legumes grown for protein-rich seeds and for nitrogen fixation; industrial crops are raw materials for industries, including oil crops (sesame, linseed) and fiber crops (cotton, sisal).
**Classify each of the four crops.** Barley is named in the unit as a cereal; linseed appears in the unit's oil crop examples; chickpea is named among pulses; sisal is listed as a fiber crop.

**Answer part (b).** Only chickpea is a leguminous pulse able to fix atmospheric nitrogen, so it is the crop that adds nitrogen to the soil; linseed, barley and sisal do not have this property in the unit.

**Answer part (c).** Sisal is a fiber crop because it is grown as an industrial raw material, while a cereal is grown for its edible starchy seed; the harvested product and the purpose of growing it are therefore completely different.

questions.q: Three Eritrean buyers place orders with a farming cooperative: an oil press needs raw material, a flour mill needs starchy grain, and a textile factory needs natural fiber. From the crops teff, niger seed, sesame, chickpea, cotton and sugarcane, (a) select one crop for each buyer and name the agronomic group it belongs to; (b) state which of the six crops are pulses and explain the soil benefit they provide; (c) name the industrial sub-group of any remaining crop that is an industrial crop but was not chosen in (a).
questions.answer: (a) Oil press: niger seed or sesame (oil crops within the industrial crops group). Flour mill: teff (cereal). Textile factory: cotton (fiber crop within the industrial crops group). (b) Chickpea is the only pulse among the six; as a leguminous plant it fixes atmospheric nitrogen in the soil and so improves soil fertility. (c) The remaining industrial crop is sugarcane, which is a sugar crop.
why: **Match each buyer to a crop group.** The unit's industrial crops include oil crops (sesame, linseed), fiber crops (cotton, sisal) and sugar crops (sugarcane, sugar beet); cereals are grown for edible starchy seeds. An oil press needs an oil crop, a flour mill needs a cereal, and a textile factory needs a fiber crop.
**Answer part (a).** Oil press: niger seed or sesame. Flour mill: teff, because teff is a cereal with starchy grain. Textile factory: cotton, because cotton is a fiber crop.

**Answer part (b).** Chickpea is the only pulse listed; the unit states that pulses are leguminous plants grown for protein-rich seeds and valued for their ability to fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil, which raises soil fertility for the next crop.
**Answer part (c).** Sugarcane was not selected by any of the three buyers and is an industrial crop of the sugar crop sub-group.
**Check that no crop is left unclassified.** Teff = cereal; niger seed and sesame = oil crops; cotton = fiber crop; sugarcane = sugar crop; chickpea = pulse. All six crops are accounted for.
